chunks: And if what we mentioned is known to be possible, how is it possible to deny the occultation of the Master of the Age (peace be upon him) in light of that? Unless the opponent is a materialist (dehri) who denies all of that and considers it impossible, in which case we do not speak with him regarding the occultation, but rather we move with him to discussing the fundamental principle of divine unity (tawhid), and that is achievable. And we only speak to those who affirm Islam and permit the possibility of that being within God's power, so we clarify for them its parallels in customary affairs.

key_terms.الْعَادَاتِ: Customary affairs/habits (referring to known natural or miraculous occurrences)
key_terms.دَهْرِيًّا: Materialist/Eternalist (one who believes in the eternity of the world without a creator)
key_terms.صَاحِبِ الزَّمَانِ: Master of the Age (referring to the 12th Imam)

ai.seo_question: How does Shia theology justify the occultation of the Imam as a plausible event?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi categorizes skeptics into materialists who deny divine power entirely and Muslims who accept it, arguing that the latter should view the Imam's occultation as a customary divine occurrence (‘adat). By shifting the debate from the extraordinary nature of the event to the established precedent of God’s power in human history, he validates the plausibility of the Hidden Imam for those already committed to Islamic theology.
